Upward convergence from Chapter 15 makes these expressions converge to MATHINLINE"\\alpha,\\beta". These limits and MATHINLINE"\\alpha+\\beta=2" hold outside one common MATHINLINE"\\mu"-null set; since MATHINLINE"P,Q\\ll\\mu", it is null for both laws. On MATHINLINE"\\alpha>0", we have MATHINLINE"W_n\\to\\beta/\\alpha<\\infty"; on MATHINLINE"\\alpha=0", we have MATHINLINE"W_n\\to\\infty". Also MATHINLINE"P(\\alpha=0)=0". Therefore
MATHBLOCK"E_PW=\\int_{\\{\\alpha>0\\}}\\beta\\,d\\mu\n=Q(\\alpha>0)\n=Q(\\limsup_n W_n<\\infty)."

The same computation on any event MATHINLINE"A" shows that the part of MATHINLINE"Q" absolutely continuous with respect to MATHINLINE"P" is MATHINLINE"W\\,dP". Only when MATHINLINE"E_PW=1" may the whole law MATHINLINE"Q" be written with this density; when MATHINLINE"E_PW=0" the laws are mutually singular. Thus a finite normalized limsup MATHINLINE"Q"-almost surely gives MATHINLINE"EW=1", hence MATHINLINE"L^1" convergence and uniform integrability of the nonnegative martingale. An infinite limsup MATHINLINE"Q"-almost surely gives MATHINLINE"EW=0", so MATHINLINE"W=0" almost surely under the original law. The latter is stronger than failure of uniform integrability; the measure-change step is essential.

Let MATHINLINE"Y_k=\\widehat L_k-1" be the off-spine children entering generation MATHINLINE"k" from its spine parent at generation MATHINLINE"k-1". These counts are iid under MATHINLINE"Q^*". With MATHINLINE"\\log^+0=0",
MATHBLOCK"E_{Q^*}\\log^+Y_1=\\frac1mE_P[L\\log^+(L-1)]."

On the right-hand side, define the whole product to be zero when MATHINLINE"L=0": it denotes MATHINLINE"\\sum_{k\\ge1}kp_k\\log^+(k-1)", with no logarithm of a negative argument. For integers MATHINLINE"k\\ge2", the difference satisfies MATHINLINE"0\\le\\log k-\\log(k-1)\\le\\log2". Since MATHINLINE"EL<\\infty", finiteness of this expectation is equivalent to MATHINLINE"E[L\\log^+L]<\\infty".

For any nonnegative MATHINLINE"V", tail-integral comparison with decreasing tail sums gives MATHINLINE"EV<\\infty" exactly when MATHINLINE"\\sum_nP(V>cn)<\\infty", for MATHINLINE"c>0". Thus for iid MATHINLINE"V_k" of finite mean, first Borel–Cantelli for all positive rational MATHINLINE"c" gives MATHINLINE"V_k/k\\to0". With infinite mean, second Borel–Cantelli for all positive integer MATHINLINE"c" gives MATHINLINE"\\limsup V_k/k=\\infty". This specific tail fact decides whether the biased tree can keep a finite normalized size.

If MATHINLINE"E[L\\log^+L]<\\infty", apply the preceding fact to MATHINLINE"V_k=\\log^+Y_k". The counts MATHINLINE"Y_k" grow subexponentially. Choose MATHINLINE"0<\\varepsilon<\\log m"; eventually MATHINLINE"Y_k\\le e^{\\varepsilon k}", so
MATHBLOCK"\\sum_{k\\ge1}\\frac{Y_k}{m^k}<\\infty\\qquad Q^*\\text{-a.s.}"

First fix any deterministic immigration sequence MATHINLINE"y_k" satisfying this summability. Attach an independent ordinary family tree to each immigrant. The off-spine population MATHINLINE"A_n" in generation MATHINLINE"n" obeys
MATHBLOCK"A_0=0,\\qquad A_{n+1}=\\sum_{j=1}^{A_n}L_{n,j}+y_{n+1}."

Consequently MATHINLINE"A_n/m^n" is a nonnegative submartingale with conditional drift MATHINLINE"y_{n+1}/m^{n+1}" and uniformly bounded mean MATHINLINE"\\sum_{k\\le n}y_k/m^k". Place the immigration sequence and the immigrants' independent original subtrees on a product space. Tonelli integrates the zero-probability failure event for each admissible immigration sequence, giving the same conclusion under MATHINLINE"Q". No finite mean of immigration counts or unproved general regular conditional distribution is needed.

We have not incorrectly called the whole MATHINLINE"W_n" a submartingale after fixing immigration: the spine's own contribution MATHINLINE"m^{-n}" decreases. The theorem must first be applied to the off-spine population. The exact identity of 20.8 now gives MATHINLINE"EW=1" and MATHINLINE"W_n\\to W" in MATHINLINE"L^1" under the original law.

If MATHINLINE"E[L\\log^+L]=\\infty", then MATHINLINE"E\\log^+Y_1=\\infty". Independent Borel–Cantelli gives MATHINLINE"\\limsup\\log^+Y_n/n=\\infty". Choosing an integer slope larger than MATHINLINE"\\log m" shows MATHINLINE"Y_n/m^n" is unbounded and tends to infinity along a subsequence.

The biased population in generation MATHINLINE"n" contains at least these MATHINLINE"Y_n" new immigrants and one spine individual. Hence MATHINLINE"\\limsup W_n=\\infty" almost surely under MATHINLINE"Q". Section 20.8 then forces MATHINLINE"W=0" almost surely under the original family law.

The original family is not being claimed to reproduce by the biased rule. Rather, the biased experiment detects precisely where its expectation hides. If families seen by a sampled offspring repeatedly overwhelm the normalization scale, the original mean cannot survive in the pathwise limit.
Assume now the finite MATHINLINE"x\\log x" condition. Limits exist simultaneously in the independent subtrees of the finitely many first-generation children. Branching decomposition gives
MATHBLOCK"W=\\frac1m\\sum_{j=1}^{L}W^{(j)}."

Put MATHINLINE"r=P(W=0)". Nonnegativity and independence give MATHINLINE"r=f(r)". Extinction is contained in MATHINLINE"W=0", so MATHINLINE"q\\le r". But MATHINLINE"EW=1" excludes MATHINLINE"r=1", and the supercritical generating function has only the fixed points MATHINLINE"q,1". Thus MATHINLINE"r=q": on survival, MATHINLINE"W>0" almost surely.
We have therefore completely proved the single-type finite-mean supercritical Kesten–Stigum criterion:
MATHBLOCK"E[L\\log^+L]<\\infty\n\\quad\\Longleftrightarrow\\quad EW=1\n\\quad\\Longleftrightarrow\\quad (W_n)\\text{ is UI},"

In this case zero limit and extinction agree modulo a null set. If the logarithmic moment is infinite, the limit is zero MATHINLINE"P"-almost surely, also when conditioned on the positive-probability survival event. Here a nontrivial limit means not identically zero: deterministic reproduction can produce the constant normalized limit one.
For example set MATHINLINE"p_2=1/2" and, for MATHINLINE"k\\ge3", take
MATHBLOCK"p_k=\\frac{c}{k^2(\\log k)^2},\\qquad\np_0=\\frac12-\\sum_{k\\ge3}p_k,\\qquad c=1/10."

These probabilities are nonnegative and sum to one, since the tail sum is less than MATHINLINE"c\\sum_{k\\ge3}k^{-2}<1/2". The mean MATHINLINE"m=1+c\\sum_{k\\ge3}[k(\\log k)^2]^{-1}" is finite and strictly above one, whereas the logarithmic moment contains the divergent series MATHINLINE"c\\sum_{k\\ge3}[k\\log k]^{-1}".

This family survives with positive probability, but MATHINLINE"Z_n/m^n\\to0" almost surely, also conditional on survival. This does not mean MATHINLINE"Z_n\\to0": mass is lost on the prescribed mean-growth scale, rather than every surviving tree turning into an empty one.

Return to MATHINLINE"m=1", exclude MATHINLINE"L\\equiv1", and assume MATHINLINE"0<\\sigma^2=\\operatorname{Var}L<\\infty". Put MATHINLINE"a_n=P(Z_n>0)". Extinction classification already gives MATHINLINE"a_n\\downarrow0", and generating-function iteration gives MATHINLINE"a_{n+1}=1-f(1-a_n)".
No third moment is assumed. Since MATHINLINE"f''(s)=E[L(L-1)s^{L-2};L\\ge2]\\uparrow\\sigma^2", the integral Taylor remainder directly gives
MATHBLOCK"a_{n+1}=a_n-\\frac{\\sigma^2}{2}a_n^2+o(a_n^2)."
Hence MATHINLINE"a_{n+1}/a_n\\to1" and MATHINLINE"a_{n+1}^{-1}-a_n^{-1}\\to\\sigma^2/2". Telescope and use Cesàro averaging to obtain
MATHBLOCK"nP(Z_n>0)\\longrightarrow\\frac2{\\sigma^2}."

This proves the finite-variance critical survival asymptotic. It does not by itself prove an exponential limit for normalized population conditional on survival; that conditional-distribution theorem needs a separate argument and cannot be inferred from one mean.

The same MATHINLINE"Z_0,Z_1,\\ldots" can arise from different parent assignments. Population records only how many individuals occupy each level, whereas the tree records their ancestry. The finite illustration preserves that distinction and shows why one spine cannot replace the entire family.

Later random-tree theory will study encodings, shapes conditional on total size, and geometric limits. This chapter establishes discrete families, population and size bias. A finite tree picture does not prove existence of a CRT, and a single-type criterion is not a theorem for multiple types, random environments or infinite-mean branching.

Mean population and survival were different questions from the beginning. The generating function makes extinction a smallest fixed point; the martingale divides average growth out of population; the spine shows how rare large families carry disproportionate average weight.

A finite logarithmic budget preserves these weights through the limit. When it fails, the family can still survive while its limit on the mean scale vanishes. Chapter 15's tail problem for fair capital has acquired a sharper genealogical answer.

Reproduction has so far occurred in orderly generations. If individuals wait and give birth at different real times, branching needs a continuous clock as well. Restart structure and memoryless waiting will supply tools for that next step.
